text:
The boys raped two girls on different occasions

A judge precising over the harrowing Hampshire rape trial handed down a sentence that sparked outrage after three boys convicted of raping two girls in separate attacks were spared jail, in part due to intellectual impairments - here are his comments in full.

The sentencing last month proved controversial after the trio were found guilty of 10 counts of rape between them for sexual assaults in 2024 and 2025. They were given youth rehabilitation orders and avoided jail.

Following sentencing, the case attracted national attention and were referred to the Court of Appeal for review. Two of the boys, aged 14 at the time, were convicted of raping a then 15-year-old girl, in November in Fording bridge.

They were also involved in the rape of a second girl, aged 14, in January 2025. A third boy, who was 13 at the time, was found guilty of rape by aiding and abetting the attack.

A full transcript of the judges sentencing remarks have been made public following a request by the BBC to have them transcribed. The remarks make mention of submissions regarding the boys' neurological impairments.

The boys, known only as J, N and E were sentenced on May 21 at the Crown Court at Southampton.

Judge Nicholas Rowaland said J, the first offender, was said to have ADHD as well as "slight cognitive difficulties," but that this did not reduce his culpability. The second defendant, known as N, was said by experts to have an IQ in the bottom 1 per cent of the country for his age group. He was also said to have ADHD and an "extreme neurological impairment" that meant he could not have ordinary schooling. His mum had described him to be like an eight-year-old boy.

Judge Rowland continued: "I am quite sure that N's culpability was reduced as result of his profound impairments. His understanding of what went on must have been far more limited than a 14 year old operating at a level without his deficits."

The youngest boy, known as E, was said to have "very low intellectual capacity" and a limited understanding of consent. Judge Rowland said the factors led him not to detain the boys as the sentencing guidelines state children in custody should be a "last resort," with a priority being rehabilitation.

"The approach to sentencing should be individualistic and focused on the child or young person, as opposed to offence-focused," he said. For a child or young person the sentence should focus on rehabilitation where possible."

The judge said evidence, and the jury's verdicts, showed that both victims initially consented to some sexual activity but that they withdrew their consent after a phone was used to film it. The judge said the initial consent could not excuse the rape.

Judge Rowland added the two lead defendants, J and N, had spend 18 and 16 months, respectively in detention at a local authority accommodation or on curfew.

He continued: "That is a significant feature when determining whether an immediate custodial sentence must follow."
